nameStory: Noah's Keyhole Limpet gets its biblical name from its scientific name 'noachina,' referring to Noah of ark fame. The 'diluvian' part of its alternate name also references the great flood, suggesting early naturalists saw something flood-related in this small sea snail. The 'keyhole' comes from the distinctive hole at the top of its cone-shaped shell, like a tiny keyhole piercing the peak.
description: Noah's Keyhole Limpet is a small marine snail that looks like a tiny volcano with a keyhole-shaped opening at its peak. Unlike typical snails that can retract into spiral shells, this creature has a cone-shaped shell that it uses like a protective helmet while clinging to rocks. The shell is usually whitish to gray and reaches about half an inch across. It's a true limpet, meaning it scrapes algae off rocks with its rough tongue-like radula.

idTips.label: Keyhole opening
idTips.description: A distinctive oval or keyhole-shaped hole sits right at the peak of the cone-shaped shell, feeling smooth to the touch around the edges

idTips.label: Cone shape
idTips.description: Shell forms a perfect little cone or volcano shape when viewed from the side, much taller than it is wide

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: Surface feels slightly rough with fine radiating ridges running from the apex down to the base, like tiny ribs

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Typically whitish, gray, or pale brown, often with darker radiating lines or bands that follow the shell's ridges

idTips.label: Rock attachment
idTips.description: Clings incredibly tightly to rocks - you'll need considerable force to pry one loose without damaging it

habitat: Look for Noah's Keyhole Limpets in the rocky intertidal zones along New England's coast, especially in areas with good wave action. They prefer hard surfaces like granite ledges, tide pool walls, and large boulders where they can scrape algae. You'll find them from the low tide line down into subtidal waters, often mixed in with other limpets, barnacles, and mussels.

seasonality.spring: Best time to search during spring tides when lowest waters expose more of their habitat. Look for them actively feeding on algae films.
seasonality.summer: Most accessible during summer low tides when tide pooling is popular. Shells may appear cleaner due to increased wave action washing away sediment.
seasonality.fall: Still findable during fall low tides, though rougher seas may make tide pooling more challenging. Shells often accumulate more marine growth.
seasonality.winter: Harder to observe due to rough winter seas and dangerous conditions, but they remain active underwater throughout the cold months.

funFact: The keyhole at the top of their shell isn't just for show - it's actually their exhaust pipe! Water flows in under the shell's edge, passes over their gills, and shoots out through the top hole, creating a perfect one-way ventilation system that works even when waves are crashing over them.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other keyhole limpets, but Noah's Keyhole Limpet has a more perfectly oval hole at the peak, while volcano limpets have more slit-like openings. Regular limpets lack any hole entirely - remember 'Noah had a key to the ark' to recall that this species needs its keyhole.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the biblical name, this species was likely named by European naturalists who saw the flood connection in its scientific name rather than any actual biblical reference. The alternate name 'diluvian puncturella' directly references the biblical deluge, showing how 19th-century scientists often incorporated religious themes into their naming conventions.
compareHints: Since Noah's Keyhole Limpet is the only Puncturella species in New England waters, compare it to other keyhole limpets in the region. It differs from most by having a more elevated, cone-like profile and a perfectly positioned oval hole at the very apex, rather than a slit or off-center opening. Its shell is also typically smaller and more delicate than the robust volcano limpet.
